key_terms.meaning: If a task can be done in one of m ways or one of n ways, and the two sets of ways do not overlap, the total is m + n ways.
If a task has k independent stages with n₁, n₂, …, n_k choices, the total is n₁ × n₂ × … × n_k ways.
An ordered arrangement of r objects picked from n distinct objects: P(n, r) = n!/(n − r)!.
An unordered selection of r objects from n: C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!) = P(n, r)/r!.
Arrangements of n objects around a ring, where rotations are the same: (n − 1)! ways.
If n + 1 objects go into n boxes, at least one box holds 2 or more objects.
If N objects go into k boxes, some box holds at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects, where ⌈x⌉ is x rounded up.
|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|, extended by subtracting odd-fold and adding even-fold overlaps.
An equation that gives aₙ in terms of earlier terms aₙ₋₁, aₙ₋₂, …, with stated initial values.
A recurrence of the form aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂ + … + c_k aₙ₋ₖ with no term free of the a's.
For aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + … + c_k aₙ₋ₖ it is r^k − c₁r^(k−1) − … − c_k = 0; its roots build the general solution.
Any one solution of a non-homogeneous recurrence, guessing the form from the forcing term.
For a sequence a₀, a₁, a₂, … it is G(x) = Σ aₙxⁿ, a power series carrying the whole sequence.
Reading aₙ back as the coefficient of xⁿ in G(x), written aₙ = [xⁿ]G(x).
A permutation of n items with no item in its own position: Dₙ = n!Σ(−1)^k/k! for k = 0 to n.
An element i with π(i) = i, i.e. it stays where it was.
The number of ways to put n identical balls into k distinct boxes is C(n + k − 1, k − 1).
If a bijection links set A to set B, then |A| = |B|; counting one set counts the other.
Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂ with F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1; the standard worked example of a linear recurrence.

takeaways: Counting starts with two rules: add when cases are disjoint, multiply when stages are independent.
Order matters gives permutations; order does not matter gives combinations, and C(n, r) = P(n, r)/r!.
The pigeonhole principle proves that a repeated or crowded case must exist, without saying which one.
Inclusion–exclusion fixes double counting by alternating subtraction and addition of overlaps.
Every linear homogeneous recurrence is solved by its characteristic roots; repeated roots add a factor of n.
A non-homogeneous recurrence is solved as homogeneous solution plus one particular solution.
A generating function turns a sequence into one algebraic object, so recurrence steps become multiplication by x.
Derangements are inclusion–exclusion in action, and their count is roughly n!/e.
Telling balls and boxes apart as identical or distinct decides which formula applies in distribution problems.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a full derivation plus verification on a small case, so write the formula, name each symbol, and show n = 1, 2, 3 to prove the formula works.

bank.q: State the sum rule and the product rule of counting. Give one Indian real-life example for each and explain why the rule applies.
outline: Sum rule: disjoint cases, total = m + n
Product rule: independent stages, total = product of choices
Example for sum: travel by train or bus between two cities
Example for product: choosing a dish and a drink from a menu
Point out the words 'or' and 'and' as the signals

bank.q: Define permutation and combination. Derive the relation C(n, r) = P(n, r)/r! and explain when each is used.
outline: P(n, r) = n!/(n − r)! built by the product rule
Every unordered selection has r! orderings
Divide P(n, r) by r! to get C(n, r)
Degree result: C(n, r) = C(n, n − r)
One example contrasting arrangement versus selection

bank.q: State the pigeonhole principle and its generalized form. Give the formula for the guaranteed minimum in a box.
outline: Basic form: n + 1 objects, n boxes → some box has ≥ 2
General form: N objects, k boxes → some box has ≥ ⌈N/k⌉
Ceiling function defined
Contrapositive phrasing: if every box has ≤ ⌈N/k⌉ − 1, contradiction

bank.q: Define a linear recurrence relation. Distinguish homogeneous from non-homogeneous, and explain order and degree with examples.
outline: Recurrence with initial conditions
Homogeneous: no term free of aₙ
Non-homogeneous: a forcing term f(n) added
Order = largest lag k; degree = power of the highest term
Examples: Fibonacci (homogeneous, order 2); aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + 3n (non-homogeneous)

bank.q: How many 4-letter words can be formed from the letters of the word 'CHENNAI' if no letter repeats? How many if the word must start with a vowel?
outline: Count distinct letters and repeated letters (N appears twice)
Apply product rule stage by stage
Vowel-first case multiplied by remaining positions
State final numbers with the reasoning

bank.q: Solve the recurrence aₙ = 5aₙ₋₁ − 6aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 1, a₁ = 4.
outline: Characteristic equation r² − 5r + 6 = 0
Roots r = 2 and r = 3, distinct
General solution aₙ = A·2ⁿ + B·3ⁿ
Use a₀, a₁ to get A = 2, B = −1
Verify for n = 2

bank.q: Using inclusion–exclusion, count the integers from 1 to 1000 that are not divisible by 2, 3 or 5.
outline: Define A, B, C as sets divisible by 2, 3, 5
|A ∪ B ∪ C| by the three-set formula
Floor values 500, 333, 200 and the pair intersections 166, 100, 66
Triple intersection ⌊1000/30⌋ = 33
Subtract the union from 1000

bank.q: Five people hand their coats to a cloakroom and get them back at random. In how many ways can every person get a wrong coat? Derive D₅ from the derangement formula.
outline: Total arrangements 5! = 120
Compute D₅ = 44
Check by inclusion–exclusion over fixed-point sets

bank.q: In how many ways can 20 identical sweets be distributed among 5 children so that each child gets at least one?
outline: Stars and bars for identical objects into distinct boxes
First give one sweet each, leaving 15
Contrast with the distinct-balls case kⁿ

bank.q: Find the generating function of the sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, … and use it to evaluate Σ n xⁿ in closed form.
outline: G(x) = Σ(n + 1)xⁿ
Relate to 1/(1 − x) = Σxⁿ
Differentiate term by term
State region of convergence |x| < 1
Homogeneous part from roots 2 and 3
Guess particular solution of form A·4ⁿ because 4 is not a root
Substitute to find A
Add and fit initial conditions
Comment on why a root equal to 4 would need a factor n

bank.q: Derive the generating function of the Fibonacci sequence from Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂ and read off Binet's formula.
outline: Multiply by xⁿ and sum over n ≥ 2
Use G(x) − F₀ − F₁x = x(G(x) − F₀) + x²G(x)
Solve G(x) = x/(1 − x − x²)
Partial fractions with roots of 1 − x − x²
Coefficient of xⁿ gives Binet's closed form

bank.q: Prove that among any n + 1 integers chosen from 1, 2, …, 2n, there are two such that one divides the other.
outline: Write each integer as odd part times a power of 2
Only n odd numbers exist below 2n
Two chosen numbers share the same odd part
The larger is then a power-of-2 multiple of the smaller
Explain why the bound n + 1 is tight

bank.q: Use inclusion–exclusion to prove the derangement formula Dₙ = n!Σ(−1)^k/k!, and show that Dₙ/n! tends to 1/e.
outline: Let Aᵢ be the set of permutations fixing element i
|Aᵢ₁ ∩ … ∩ Aᵢⱼ| = (n − j)!
C(n, j) such intersections, alternating signs
Factor n! to obtain the series
Recognise the exponential series for −1

glossary.def: A rule that gives the size of a set of outcomes without listing them.
Two sets with no element in common, so their sizes add cleanly.
The product 1 × 2 × … × n, with 0! defined as 1.
The smallest integer greater than or equal to x.
The largest integer less than or equal to x.
C(n, r) = C(n − 1, r − 1) + C(n − 1, r), Pascal's rule.
C(m + n, r) = Σ C(m, i)·C(n, r − i) over valid i.
Counting the unwanted outcomes and subtracting from the total.
Another name for the pigeonhole principle.
The set of elements in at least one of the given sets.
The set of elements common to all the given sets.
A function whose image equals its whole codomain; used in counting onto placements.
Starting values such as a₀ and a₁ that fix one sequence out of a recurrence's family.
The family of all sequences satisfying a recurrence before initial values are applied.
A root r of multiplicity m in the characteristic equation; it contributes terms nⁱrⁿ for i = 0 to m − 1.
The function f(n) on the right side of a non-homogeneous recurrence.
An infinite sum of the form Σ aₙxⁿ.
A power series treated as algebra only, with convergence not required.
Splitting a rational generating function into simpler pieces whose coefficients are known.
The sequence cₙ = Σ aᵢbₙ₋ᵢ, whose generating function is the product A(x)B(x).
Objects treated as indistinguishable, so only counts per box matter.
Objects treated as labelled, so which object goes where matters.
The number of ways to split n distinct objects into k non-empty unlabelled boxes.
Distributions of n distinct balls into k distinct boxes with no box empty: k!·S(n, k).
